content: The dossier on behalf of the country includes a field visit and provides recommendations to the World Health Organization (WHO) regarding whether to support or reject the national assessment of transmission interruption. This decision directly impacts the national claim of having interrupted the transmission of the onchocercal parasite. The status of elimination can only be granted to a country by the WHO Director-General after all identified foci under long-term, continuous ivermectin treatment have been verified as free of transmission. Additionally, sufficient evidence must be provided to confirm that all areas of potential transmission have been identified, ensuring that the transmission of Onchocerca volvulus no longer occurs in the country. This determination is based on the report of the international verification team. The elimination of O. volvulus transmission cannot be verified until a sufficient number of years of ivermectin treatment and post-treatment surveillance have been completed. In cases where transmission persists in neighboring countries, WHO may withhold acknowledgment of elimination for a country until the surrounding areas have also interrupted transmission. If elimination is documented through appropriate testing of black flies and corroborated by serological evaluation of children under 10 years of age, the national program establishes a post-elimination surveillance system. This system is designed to detect any potential resurgence of parasite transmission, whether through recrudescence or reintroduction, in previously endemic, non-endemic, or areas at risk of imported cases. Post-elimination surveillance focuses on entomological assessments, demonstrating the absence of infective-stage larvae of O. volvulus in vector populations using O-150 PCR with O. volvulus-specific DNA probes. It is anticipated that new discoveries, such as improved diagnostic assays or novel interventions, will emerge. These innovations should be tested and validated under field conditions for their applicability and, if deemed suitable, incorporated into revised guidelines for future consideration. Further clarification on the co-endemicity of onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis is expected as more programs encounter this situation and specific lessons are learned. Metrics for onchocerciasis control have been extensively supported by field and modeling-based research. Widely used models include ONCHOSIM, SIMON, and the EuSimOn model, refined for the Americas and currently employed by the Onchocerciasis Elimination Program for the Americas (OEPA). Independent approaches have examined questions relevant to elimination, such as the persistence of onchocerciasis under varying ecological conditions and the feasibility of elimination through vector control and mass drug administration (MDA). Despite advancements in understanding onchocerciasis control and elimination, current and future strategies face challenges, including the impact of macrofilaricides on long-term ivermectin distribution and the extent to which this intervention shortens the duration of annual, biannual, or quarterly MDA until elimination is achieved. The guidelines for stopping mass drug administration and verifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis will be issued and launched at a suitable event to maximize visibility. The WHO Secretariat will collaborate with neglected tropical disease focal points in regional offices and country offices of onchocerciasis-endemic countries to ensure wide dissemination of the guidelines to end-users, including national program managers and their implementing partners. The guidelines will also be made available electronically on the WHO website in an easily downloadable format.
